title: Tenant infra extension strategies for private VPC deployments
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: Customers deploying Redwood Private into their VPCs require per-tenant customizations (networking, routing, IAM bindings, optional connectors) without forking core Terraform modules for every customer. We need a set of practical, supported customization patterns that: (1) minimize drift from upstream modules, (2) enable safe upgrades and rollbacks, (3) support tenant-local overrides for sensitive values, and (4) provide a reliable way to run health checks and smoke tests post-upgrade.

Scope: Patterns and examples for module composition, overlay file layout, variable scoping, provider aliasing, state/backends, upgrade/canary strategy, CI gating for plan/apply, and health-check automation. Not covering infra provisioning beyond Terraform (eg. in-cluster manifests).

Design summary: We recommend a 3-layer approach: 
1) core-modules (redwood/terraform-modules): canonical, versioned modules that own resource shapes and public variable contracts.
2) wrapper modules (customer-specific wrappers): small modules that compose core modules and expose a thin surface for tenant overrides and glue logic.
3) tenant overlays (tenant-configs): lightweight directories per-customer that supply tfvars, provider alias maps, and optional patch files (generated) to customize behavior.

Key patterns and rationale:
- Wrapper modules instead of forking: Create minimal wrapper modules per product-area (eg. redwood.vpc, redwood.loadbalancer) that call into core modules. Wrappers translate tenant intent into core inputs (eg. map->list transformation) and can contain compatibility code for older core module versions. This keeps tenant code small and makes upstream upgrades simpler.

- Overlay layout recommendation:
  infra/
    modules/                 # local thin wrappers (checked into redwood-tenant-repo)
    core_ref/                # pointer file with module source+version
    tenants/
      customer-acme/
        backend.tf            # remote state config (S3/GCS) with tenant-specific keys and lock config
        providers.tf          # provider aliases and region/account mappings
        main.tf               # invokes wrapper modules
        tenant.tfvars         # tenant overrides and secrets references (KMS/HSM keys stored in secrets manager)
        ci/                   # per-tenant CI workflows for plan/apply and smoke tests

- Variables & secrets: Secrete values (certs, keystores) should never be checked into overlays. Use references to the customer's secret store (eg. arn:aws:secretsmanager:...) and keep stubbed tfvars in repo pointing at secret ids. For local testing we provide a "secrets-sample.tfvars" that is ignored in real deployments.

- Provider aliasing and multi-account support: Use provider aliases declared at the overlay level. Wrapper modules accept an optional provider alias map to route sub-resources to the correct account/role. Example: provider "aws" { alias = "ops" } and pass providers = { aws = aws.ops } at the module call site. This avoids hardcoding account IDs in core modules.

- State management: Use a dedicated remote backend per-tenant (unique key prefix) to avoid accidental cross-tenant state collisions. Use per-tenant DynamoDB/State locking for AWS, or GCS+locks for GCP. Add an explicit "state-migration" guide in the repo when we change state key formats.

- Versioning and upgrade strategy: Always pin core module sources with a version tag (git tag or registry version). The wrapper modules can contain compatibility shims to accept older var shapes. Upgrade flow: 
  a) Create a branch that updates core module references in wrappers and runs an automated plan against a small set of canary tenants.
  b) Run plan-only CI for all tenants, collect diffs and impact metrics (resource count, replacement risk).
  c) Execute apply for canaries and run health checks; if stable, schedule rolling apply for the rest with a staged cadence.
  d) If breaking changes are required, publish a migration helper module that maps old state to new resources (see "compat modules" below).

- Canary tenant pattern: Maintain a small group (1-3 tenants or internal QA tenants) designated as canaries. The CI config supports a targeted apply action that only runs against a tenant list (via env var TENANTS=canary1,canary2) and emits telemetry to the deployment dashboard. Only after canary success is the batch applied to the rest.

- Compatibility/compat modules: When module interfaces change (eg. we split resource into two), publish a compat wrapper that accepts the old inputs and synthesizes the new inputs, or maintain a migration-only module that renames resources in state. Keep these compat modules short-lived but well-documented.

- Patching vs generated overlays: For complex per-tenant differences (eg. unusual NACL rules), prefer generating a small patch file (generated by a utility in redwood/infra-tools) and committing it to the tenant's repo as part of the change branch. The generator can be used to validate invariants. Avoid ad-hoc manual edits in core modules.

- CI & gating: All tenant changes must be plan-reviewed. CI should run terraform init/validate/plan with a stable lockfile (terraform.lock.hcl) and required_providers pinned. Use a "plan artifact" upload so reviewers can inspect diffs. Applies must be gated: only automation with approved run tokens or an engineer with required RBAC can run apply.

- Health checks and smoke tests: After apply, run an automated smoke test pipeline per-tenant that executes: 
  - Terraform external data source-driven checks (null_resource triggers that call small scripts), and/or 
  - GitHub Action step that runs scripts in the tenant repo which call the deployed endpoints (eg. /healthz, /metrics, basic inference request) and validate latency and correctness.
  - Push results to a deployment dashboard; transient failures should cause automatic rollback plan generation.

- Drift detection and periodic checks: Run a scheduled terraform plan (nightly/weekly) for each tenant and report unexpected diffs. For reduction of noise, only surface diffs for resources flagged as "managed_by_redwood" via tags.

- Policy & safety: Integrate policy checks (OPA/Terraform Sentinel or Conftest) in CI to enforce allowed CIDR ranges, required tags, and that no public S3 buckets are created. Make policies configurable per-tenant with a policy overlay in the tenant directory.

- Secrets of scale: For large customer fleets, recommend a hybrid approach where small tenants are managed by a centralized repo/workspace with per-tenant workspace state, and large customers get a dedicated repo and state backend. Document the threshold and a migration playbook.

Examples (short snippets):
- wrapper module call (main.tf) example:

module "redwood_vpc" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infrastructure-modules.git//vpc?ref=v1.7.2"
  name   = var.tenant_name
  cidrs  = var.vpc_cidrs
  providers = { aws = aws.tenant }
}

- provider aliasing (providers.tf):

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "tenant"
  region = var.region
  assume_role { arn = var.cross_account_role }
}

- post-apply smoke test (github action snippet):

- name: Run tenant smoke tests
  run: |
    ./ci/run_smoke_tests.sh --tenant ${TENANT}

Trade-offs and known risks:
- Trade-off: Wrapper modules add extra indirection and slight cognitive overhead. Benefit: upgrade isolation and minimal per-tenant diffs.
- Risk: Divergence if tenants keep long-lived manual overrides in overlays. Mitigation: periodic repository audits and drift alerts.
- Risk: Large-scale applies can cause burst capacity issues. Mitigation: staged rolling applies and autoscaling pre-warm policies.

Next steps / action items:
- Implement reference wrapper modules for vpc and loadbalancer (ENG-9950).
- Create tenant generator utility for patch creation and validation (ENG-9962).
- Add canary CI workflow templates to the infra-ci repo and document in Confluence (link below).
acceptance_criteria: Canonical wrapper modules exist for core product areas (VPC, LB, IAM) and are published with semver tags.
Overlay repo layout documented with examples and CI templates in the infra-ci repo.
Canary apply workflow implemented and exercised against internal canary tenants.
Post-apply smoke tests integrated and results visible on the deployment dashboard.
Upgrade playbook exists describing plan-only PRs, canary apply, metrics to observe, and rollback steps.
